title: Tests in plain words
objectives: Explain a p-value, power and a multiple-testing correction without jargon.

screens.title: Forty heads
screens.prose: This lesson takes about 25 minutes, two minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. A coin lands heads 40 times in 64 flips. If it is fair, heads has mean 32 and standard deviation $\sqrt{64 \times 0.5 \times 0.5} = 4$.

derive.caption: Shaded: results at least as far from 32 as {{h}} heads.

screens.question: How many standard deviations above 32 is 40? That number is $z$.

hints.text: Take 32 from 40, then divide.
The standard deviation is 4, not 16.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation.

byKey.raw: You stopped at the gap of 8 heads. Divide it by the standard deviation, 4.
byKey.var: You divided by the variance, 16. Divide by its square root, 4.

explain.text: $z = (40 - 32)/4 = 2$. The shaded tails are every result at least 2 standard deviations from 32, either way.

screens.title: The p-value on the curve
screens.prose: The p-value is the shaded area: how often a fair coin does at least this well, either way.

derive.caption: Shaded: results at least as far from 32 as {{h}} heads.

screens.question: Using the normal curve, with no continuity correction, what is the two-sided p-value?

hints.text: Two tails beyond $z = \pm 2$.
Double it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two tails beyond $\pm 2$.

byKey.exact: That is the exact binomial. The question said use the normal curve.
byKey.one: You gave one tail. Two-sided counts results this far below 50 as well.

explain.text: Each tail beyond 2 has 0.0228, so the two-sided p is 0.0455. A fair coin lands this far from 32 about once in 22 tries.

screens.title: Exact or normal
screens.prose: The exact binomial counts every outcome at 24 or below and 40 or above. It gives 0.0599, with one tail 0.0300.
screens.question: The interviewer asks: is 40 heads significant at 5%? What do you say?

options.text: It depends on the method, so I say which one I used
Yes: the normal curve gives $p = 0.0455$, below 5%
options.why: That is one method. The exact test gives 0.0599, above 5%, so say which you used.

options.text: No: the exact test gives $p = 0.0599$, above 5%
options.why: That is one method. The normal curve gives 0.0455, so say which you used.

options.text: Yes: 40 is well above 32, the mean for a fair coin
options.why: Distance alone says nothing. It has to be measured against the spread, 4.

hints.text: Compare the two p-values with 0.05.
They fall on opposite sides of 0.05.
A borderline answer names its method.

feedback.correct: Name the method; the answer sits on the line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The two methods disagree here.

byKey.yes: You trusted the normal curve alone. The exact test lands above 5%.

explain.text: The exact two-sided p is 0.0599 and the normal one 0.0455. They straddle 5%, so a borderline call depends on the method. Say which you used; a continuity correction brings the normal close to the exact figure.

screens.title: Power
screens.prose: Now test a mean: $\sigma = 1$, $n = 25$, two-sided at 5%. The sample mean has standard error $1/\sqrt{25} = 0.2$, so we reject beyond $\pm 1.96 \times 0.2 = \pm 0.392$. The true mean is 0.5.

state.caption: Solid: the null. Dashed: the truth. Shaded: where we reject.

screens.question: How often does the test reject when the true mean is 0.5?

hints.text: Under the truth, how far is 0.392 from 0.5?
$\Phi(0.54)$, plus a negligible far tail.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance, under the true mean, of landing beyond 0.392.

byKey.alpha: That is the false positive rate under the null. Power is computed under the truth.
byKey.conf: That is one minus the level. Power depends on the effect size and $n$.
byKey.half: You took the chance of landing above the true mean. The cut-off is 0.392, a little below it.

explain.text: Under the truth the cut-off 0.392 is 0.54 standard errors below 0.5, so power is $\Phi(0.54) = 0.7054$. For 80% we need $n = ((1.96 + 0.84)/0.5)^2 = 31.4$, so 32 (power 0.8074).

screens.title: What p = 0.04 says
screens.prose: A colleague reports $p = 0.04$ and says: so there is a 4% chance the null is true. The shaded area is that p-value on the null curve.
screens.question: Which reading of $p = 0.04$ is right?

options.text: Under the null, a result this extreme turns up 4% of the time
There is a 4% chance that the null hypothesis is true
options.why: You read the p-value as the chance of the null. It assumes the null and says nothing about its chance.

options.text: There is a 96% chance that the effect we found is real
options.why: That is the same misreading turned round. The p-value is computed as if the null held.

options.text: A repeat of the study would give about $p = 0.04$ again
options.why: A p-value varies from sample to sample. A repeat can land far above or below 0.04.

hints.text: On which curve is the shaded area computed?
It is the null curve: the null is assumed.
So $p$ is a chance about the data, given the null.

feedback.correct: Correct: it is a statement about the data under the null.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The p-value assumes the null.

byKey.null: You read the p-value as the chance of the null. It assumes the null and says nothing about its chance.

explain.text: The shaded area is computed on the null curve, so the null is assumed throughout. The chance the null is true needs a prior, which the p-value never uses. Say it as: luck alone does this well 4% of the time.

screens.title: A Sharpe ratio as a test
screens.prose: A strategy has an annual Sharpe ratio of 1 over four years. Its yearly returns are close to independent. The $t$ statistic of its mean return is the Sharpe ratio times the square root of the years.
screens.question: What is $t$?

hints.text: $t = \text{SR} \times \sqrt{T}$.
$T = 4$ years.
$1 \times \sqrt{4}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the Sharpe ratio by the square root of the years.

byKey.one: You took the Sharpe ratio as the $t$ statistic. It grows with the square root of the years.
byKey.four: You multiplied by the years. The $t$ statistic grows with $\sqrt{T}$.

explain.text: $t = 1 \times \sqrt{4} = 2$, so $p \approx 0.0455$, a borderline result. Halving the Sharpe ratio needs four times the years for the same $t$.

screens.title: Ten looks
screens.prose: Ten independent tests, each at 5%, and no real effect anywhere. The bars count the false positives.
screens.question: What is the chance of at least one false positive?

hints.text: Find the chance of no false positive first.
Each test stays quiet with chance 0.95.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take one minus the chance that all ten stay quiet.

byKey.sum: You added ten chances of 5%. That counts overlaps twice; use $1 - 0.95^{10}$.
byKey.one: That is the chance for one test. With ten, false positives pile up.

explain.text: $1 - 0.95^{10} = 0.4013$. Bonferroni tests each at $0.05/10 = 0.005$, which brings the overall chance back below 5%.

screens.title: Three corrections
screens.prose: Five strategies give the p-values below. Bonferroni compares each with $0.05/5$. Holm raises the bar step by step and stops at the first miss. Benjamini-Hochberg takes the largest rank $k$ with $p_{(k)} \le 0.05k/5$.

state.caption: Sorted p-values and each method's bar at 5%. Bonf. is Bonferroni; BH is Benjamini-Hochberg.

screens.question: How many does each method reject?

hints.text: Bonferroni: count the p-values at or below 0.01.
Holm: walk down the ranks and stop at the first $p$ above its bar.
BH: find the largest rank whose $p$ is under its bar.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each $p$ with its own column.

byKey.r0c1: Bonferroni: only 0.001 and 0.008 are at or below 0.01.
byKey.r1c1: Holm: 0.001, 0.008 and 0.012 pass their bars; 0.03 is above 0.025, so it stops.
byKey.r2c1: BH: rank 4 has $0.03 \le 0.04$, so the first four are rejected.

explain.text: Bonferroni rejects 2, Holm 3 and Benjamini-Hochberg 4. Holm controls the same error as Bonferroni with more power. BH controls the false discovery rate instead, a looser target.

screens.title: Tests in plain words
screens.prose: A p-value is how often luck alone does at least this well. Power is how often a real effect of a stated size is caught. A correction lowers the bar when you look many times: $$P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m, \qquad \alpha_{\text{Bonferroni}} = \alpha/m.$$
screens.question: What Bonferroni level keeps twenty tests at 5% overall?

hints.text: Divide the level by the number of tests.

byKey.same: You kept 5% for each test, which lets false positives pile up.

explain.text: $0.05/20 = 0.0025$. Each test faces a stricter bar, so the family as a whole stays near 5%.

screens.title: The best of fifty backtests
screens.prose: A researcher backtests fifty strategies and shows you the best, with $t = 3$. Its two-sided p-value on the normal curve is 0.0027.
screens.question: What is its Bonferroni-adjusted p-value, $50 \times p$?

hints.text: Multiply the p-value by the number of tries.
Then compare with 0.05.

byKey.raw: You kept the raw p-value. The best of fifty needs the correction.
byKey.sidak: That is the Šidák value, $1 - (1 - p)^{50}$. It is a fair answer, but the question asked for $50 \times p$.

explain.text: $50 \times 0.0027 = 0.135$, and Šidák gives 0.1264. Either way the best of fifty is not significant at 5%. Luck alone gives a best this good about one time in eight.

screens.title: The follow-up: say it to a portfolio manager
screens.prose: The interviewer says: now explain that result to a portfolio manager in two sentences.
screens.question: Which wording would you use?

options.text: After fifty tries, luck alone gives a best this good about one time in eight. We would test it on fresh data first.
The best strategy has only a 0.27% chance of being a fluke. So we should put it into production next week.
options.why: That reads the p-value as the chance of a fluke and ignores the fifty tries.

options.text: The result is significant at $p = 0.0027$, far below 5%. So the strategy has a real edge.
options.why: That quotes the raw p-value. After fifty tries the corrected value is 0.135.

options.text: Its Sharpe ratio is three, so it is a strong strategy. We should trade it at full size.
options.why: A $t$ statistic of 3 is not a Sharpe ratio of 3, and luck explains it here.

hints.text: Which wording mentions the fifty tries?
The adjusted p-value is 0.135, about one in eight.
A good answer also says what to do next.

feedback.correct: Plain words, the number of tries, and the next step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A good answer allows for the fifty tries.

byKey.fluke: You read the p-value as the chance of a fluke. It is not, and the fifty tries change it.

explain.text: The right wording names the fifty tries and gives the chance in plain words. It ends with the next step: fresh data. The other wordings misread the p-value or ignore the search.

ideas: A p-value is how often luck alone does at least this well, assuming no effect.
Power is how often a real effect of a stated size is caught; it grows with $n$.
With $m$ looks, false positives pile up as $1 - (1 - \alpha)^m$; correct by Bonferroni, Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg.
summary.trap: $p = 0.04$ is not a 4% chance that the null is true.

quiz.question: A test gives $p = 0.03$. Which sentence is right?

options.text: With no effect, data this extreme turn up 3% of the time
There is a 3% chance that there is no effect at all
options.why: That reads the p-value as the chance of the null, which it assumes.

options.text: There is a 97% chance that the effect is real
The effect is large, since the p-value is small
options.why: A tiny effect in a huge sample can also give $p = 0.03$.

feedback.correct: Right: a statement about the data, given the null.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The p-value assumes the null.

explain.text: The p-value is computed as if there were no effect. It says how surprising the data are then.

quiz.prose: $\sigma = 2$, $n = 16$, a two-sided test at 5%, and a true mean of 1.
quiz.question: What is the power?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how many standard errors the true mean sits from 0.

byKey.alpha: That is the level, the false positive rate. Power is computed under the truth.
byKey.phi2: You took $\Phi(2)$. Subtract the 1.96 cut-off first: $\Phi(2 - 1.96)$.

explain.text: The standard error is $2/\sqrt{16} = 0.5$, so the true mean sits 2 standard errors out. Power is $\Phi(2 - 1.96) = 0.516$, barely better than a coin flip.

quiz.question: Forty tests at 5% overall. What level does Bonferroni give each test?
A Sharpe ratio of 0.5 a year over 16 years. What is $t$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by the square root of the years.

byKey.sr: The Sharpe ratio is not the $t$ statistic. Scale it by $\sqrt{T}$.

explain.text: $0.5 \times \sqrt{16} = 2$. A modest Sharpe ratio needs many years to become significant.
